source_text: Μεγαλειότερα μὲν οὖν πάσης ἀνθρωπείου διδασκαλίας φαίνεται τὰ ἡμέτερα διὰ τοῦ τὸ λογικὸν τὸ ὅλον τὸν φανέντα δι᾿ ἡμᾶς Χριστὸν γεγονέναι καὶ σῶμα καὶ λόγον καὶ ψυχήν. Ὅσα γὰρ καλῶς ἀεὶ ἐφθέγξαντο καὶ εὗρον οἱ φιλοσοφήσαντες ἢ νομοθετήσαντες, κατὰ λόγου μέρος δι᾿ εὑρέσεως καὶ θεωρίας ἐστὶ πονηθέντα αὐτοῖς. Ἐπειδὴ δὲ οὐ πάντα τὰ τοῦ λόγου ἐγνώρισαν, ὅς ἐστι Χριστός, καὶ ἐναντία ἑαυτοῖς πολλάκις εἶπον. Καὶ οἱ προγεγενημένοι τοῦ Χριστοῦ, κατὰ τὸ ἀνθρώπινον λόγῳ πειραθέντες τὰ πράγματα θεωρῆσαι καὶ ἐλέγξαι, ὡς ἀσεβεῖς καὶ περίεργοι εἰς δικαστήρια ἤχθησαν. Ὁ πάντων δὲ αὐτῶν εὐτονώτερος πρὸς τοῦτο γενόμενος Σωκράτης τὰ αὐτὰ ἡμῖν ἐνεκλήθη· καὶ γὰρ ἔφασαν αὐτὸν καινὰ δαιμόνια εἰσφέρειν, καὶ οὓς ἡ πόλις νομίζει θεοὺς μὴ ἡγεῖσθαι αὐτόν. Ὁ δὲ δαίμονας μὲν τοὺς φαύλους καὶ τοὺς πράξαντας ὰ ἔφασαν οἱ ποιηταί, ἐκβαλὼν τῆς πολιτείας καὶ Ὅμηρον καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους ποιητάς, παραιτεῖσθαι τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἐδίδαξε, πρὸς θεοῦ δὲ τοῦ ἀγνώστου αὐτοῖς διὰ λόγου ζητήσεως ἐπίγνωσιν προὐτρέπετο, εἰπών· „Τὸν δὲ πατέρα καὶ δημιουργὸν πάντων οὔθ᾿ εὑρεῖν ῥᾴδιον, οὔθ᾿ εὑρόντα εἰς πάντας εἰπεῖν ἀσφαλές“. Ἅ ὁ ἡμέτερος Χριστὸς διὰ τῆς ἑαυτοῦ δυνάμεως ἔπραξε. Σωκράτει μὲν γὰρ οὐδεὶς ἐπείσθη ὑπὲρ τούτου τοῦ δόγματος ἀποθνήσκειν· Χριστῷ δέ, τῷ καὶ ὑπὸ Σωκράτους ἀπὸ μέρους γνωσθέντι (λόγος γὰρ ἦν καὶ ἔστιν ὁ ἐν παντὶ ὤν, καὶ διὰ τῶν προφητῶν προειπὼν τὰ μέλλοντα γίνεσθαι καὶ δι᾿ ἑαυτοῦ ὁμοιοπαθοῦς γενομένου καὶ διδάξαντος ταῦτα), οὐ φιλόσοφοι οὐδὲ φιλόλογοι μόνον ἐπείσθησαν, ἀλλὰ καὶ χειροτέχναι καὶ παντελῶς ἰδιῶται, καὶ δόξης καὶ φόβου καὶ θανάτου καταφρονήσαντες· ἐπειδὴ δύναμίς ἐστι τοῦ ἀῤῥήτου πατρὸς καὶ οὐχὶ ἀνθρωπείου λόγου τὰ σκεύη.
thought_title: Christ is the whole Word, greater than all human teaching
orientation: Justin is addressing the Roman Senate and people, arguing that Christian teaching surpasses all human philosophy because Christ is the whole Word of God.
pass_a_gloss: More majestic than all human teaching appear our things, because of this: the whole Word, the one who appeared for us, Christ, has become both body and word and soul. For whatever things the philosophers or lawgivers ever spoke well and found, by a part of the Word through discovery and contemplation was worked out by them. But since they did not know all the things of the Word, who is Christ, they often said things contrary to themselves. And those who lived before Christ, having attempted according to the human standard by reason to contemplate and examine the matters, were brought into courts as impious and meddlesome. The one who became more vigorous than all of them toward this, Socrates, was accused of the same things as us; for they said that he introduced new demons, and that he did not consider the gods whom the city considers gods. But he, having cast out of the state the demons, the wicked ones and the ones who did the things which the poets said, both Homer and the other poets, taught people to reject them, and toward knowledge of the God unknown to them through rational inquiry he urged them, saying: 'The father and maker of all things is neither easy to find, nor, having found him, safe to tell to all.' These things our Christ did through his own power. For no one was persuaded by Socrates to die for this doctrine; but by Christ, who was also known in part by Socrates (for he was and is the Word who is in everyone, and who foretold through the prophets the things that were going to happen and through himself becoming subject to like passions and teaching these things), not only philosophers and lovers of words were persuaded, but also craftsmen and altogether uneducated people, having despised glory and fear and death; since he is power of the ineffable father and not the vessels of human reason.

choices.why: Keeps the neuter substantive force of λογικόν as 'the rational principle' rather than collapsing it into 'Word' (λόγος), preserving Justin's distinction between the rational principle and the Word who is Christ.

choices.term: καὶ σῶμα καὶ λόγον καὶ ψυχήν
choices.english: both body and word and soul
choices.why: Literal rendering of the threefold nature Justin attributes to Christ's incarnation; 'word' here is λόγος in its ordinary sense, not the divine title, so it is not capitalized.

choices.english: by a part of the Word
choices.why: Renders the partitive genitive literally; 'Word' is capitalized because λόγος here refers to the divine Word, consistent with the glossary.
rejected: according to a portion of reason
by a share of the Logos

choices.why: The adverbial accusative with κατά is rendered literally to show that their attempt was merely human, not by divine power.
ἄρρητος means 'unspeakable, ineffable'; 'ineffable' preserves the sense of that which cannot be uttered, fitting Justin's theology of the unbegotten Father.
Literal rendering of σκεύη as 'vessels' or 'instruments'; Justin contrasts Christ as power of the Father with mere human instruments.

pass_b_english: Our teachings, then, appear more majestic than every human teaching, because the whole Word, Christ who appeared for our sake, became body and word and soul. For whatever the philosophers and lawgivers ever spoke or discovered that was good, they worked out by a part of the Word through discovery and contemplation. But since they did not know everything of the Word, who is Christ, they often said things contrary to one another.

And those who lived before Christ, when they tried to examine and refute things by reason according to the human standard, were brought into courts as impious and meddlesome. Socrates, who was more vigorous than all of them in this, was accused of the same things as we are; for they said that he was introducing new demons and that he did not regard the gods the city recognized. But he cast out of the commonwealth the wicked demons and those who did the things the poets said, he taught people to reject Homer and the other poets, and he urged them to gain knowledge of the God who was unknown to them through the search of the Word, saying: "The father and maker of all is neither easy to find, nor safe to tell to all when found." These things our Christ accomplished by his own power.

For no one was persuaded by Socrates to die for this doctrine; but by Christ, who was known in part even by Socrates (for he was and is the Word who is in everyone, and who foretold through the prophets the things that were to happen, and through himself became subject to the same sufferings and taught these things), not only philosophers and scholars were persuaded, but also craftsmen and entirely uneducated people, and they despised glory and fear and death; since he is the power of the ineffable Father, and not of human reason.

problems.quote: the whole rational principle became Christ, who appeared for our sake, and became body and word and soul
problems.source_quote: τὸ λογικὸν τὸ ὅλον τὸν φανέντα δι᾿ ἡμᾶς Χριστὸν γεγονέναι καὶ σῶμα καὶ λόγον καὶ ψυχήν
problems.why: Renders λογικόν as 'rational principle' and λόγον as 'word', violating glossary 'Word' for λόγος. Also Christ didn't 'become' λόγον; he is the Word who became body, word, soul.
problems.fix: the whole Word, Christ who appeared for our sake, became body and Word and soul
problems.ruling: Greek says Christ appears through the whole rational, not that the rational principle became Christ

problems.quote: and taught people to reject Homer and the other poets
problems.source_quote: παραιτεῖσθαι τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἐδίδαξε, πρὸς θεοῦ δὲ... προὐτρέπετο
problems.why: The verb παραιτεῖσθαι governs both the demons/poets and the people; Socrates taught people to reject the demons and Homer, not 'taught to reject people'.
problems.fix: he taught people to reject Homer and the other poets
problems.ruling: Greek: Socrates taught people to reject demons, not Homer and poets

problems.quote: since he is the power of the ineffable Father, and not the vessels of human word
problems.source_quote: ἐπειδὴ δύναμίς ἐστι τοῦ ἀῤῥήτου πατρὸς καὶ οὐχὶ ἀνθρωπείου λόγου τὰ σκεύη
problems.why: Subject shifts: 'he is the power' but 'not the vessels' makes no sense. Source says the vessels (people persuaded) are power of the Father, not of human word.
problems.fix: since they are vessels of the power of the ineffable Father, and not of human word
problems.ruling: Greek: power of Father applies to vessels, not ‘he’ being power and not vessels

problems.quote: when they tried to examine and refute things by the human standard through the Word
problems.source_quote: κατὰ τὸ ἀνθρώπινον λόγῳ πειραθέντες τὰ πράγματα θεωρῆσαι καὶ ἐλέγξαι
problems.why: Greek says “according to the human standard” without mentioning the Word; English adds “through the Word”, altering agency.
problems.fix: when they tried to examine and refute things according to the human standard
problems.ruling: Greek has κατὰ τὸ ἀνθρώπινον λόγῳ; English adds 'through the Word', wrongly importing λόγος as divine Word rather than human reason.

fixed: The glossary issue is not a translation problem in this passage; the English already uses 'the Word' consistently.

The phrase 'became body and Word and soul' is a literal rendering of the source; the source itself says Christ became body and word and soul, so the English is accurate. I have adjusted 'Word' to lowercase 'word' to reflect the source's use of λόγον as a component of human nature, not the divine Word.

The quotation is from Plato's Timaeus 28c, but the source attributes it to Socrates with the phrase 'εἰπών' (saying). The English already renders this as a direct quotation from Socrates, which matches the source. I have adjusted 'declare' to 'tell' to match the source's 'εἰπεῖν' more closely.

The English 'and not the vessels of human reason' is grammatically awkward because 'he' cannot be 'vessels.' The smallest fix is to make the contrast parallel: 'and not of human reason.'
